back: Dividing a program into fixed-size pages and memory into frames of the same size; any page can go in any frame.
Records the frame that holds each page of a process.
Dividing a program into logical segments of different sizes, each with a base address and a limit.
Using the disk as an extension of main memory so a program can be larger than the RAM.
A request for a page that is not in main memory; the page is loaded from the disk.
Frame number × page size + offset; page = logical address ÷ page size, offset = the remainder.
FIFO replaces the oldest page, LRU the least recently used, optimal the page needed furthest in the future (not possible in practice).
Constant swapping of pages between disk and memory with very little useful work; reduced by closing programs or adding RAM.
Pages: equal size, physical. Segments: unequal size, logical, with base and limit.
